### new-feature-bug-hunt

*Sumber: `installed` - `skills/02-recon-targeting/new-feature-bug-hunt/SKILL.md`*

> Use when hunting bugs in newly released features.

# Bug Hunting in New Features

Fresh features are where the bugs are: least review, most rushing, deadlines that
skip edge cases. The old app has been picked over by hundreds of hunters for
years; a feature released last week has been touched by almost nobody.

## When to Use

Load this when starting a hunt on a target that just shipped something — a new
program/deployment, an upgrade, a passed governance proposal, a new web feature,
or a newly added scope asset. Also use it whenever a program's changelog,
release notes, blog, JS bundle, or scope page changes.

**Surface routing:** the concrete workflow below (blockscout age check, fork PoC,
keccak signature diffs) is CHAIN-specific. For a web / REST API / OAuth / hosted
MCP target, the consistency question here still drives the hunt, but the recon
probe matrix, account handoff, and PoC harness live in **web-api-bounty-hunt** —
load that instead of applying the chain mechanics to a web surface.

## The one question that drives everything

For every new action that moves money or changes state, ask:

> Does the new feature follow the same rules as the old ones?

Same permissions, same checks, same ownership, same accounting, same pause,
same event shape. Usually somebody forgot exactly one. Find it.

## Workflow

1. **Discovery** — find what is new. Changelog, release notes, blog/announcement,
   scope page, JS bundle diff (web); new program ID / proxy impl / passed
   proposal / new deployment (chain).
   For web3 contests, read each platform's own live-competition page (Immunefi,
   Cantina, Sherlock, ...). A generic bounty aggregator RSS feed is dominated by
   web2 scope changes and will miss web3 launches — use it only as a secondary signal.
   **Verify the real age before investing — a platform's "launched <30d" / "New" /
   "New scope" badge dates the LISTING, not the CODE.** Two checks decide it, and
   one cost line decides whether it pays at all:
   - source-code scope: the GitHub API on the PINNED commits (`git log`,
     `api.github.com/repos/<org>/<repo>/commits/<sha>`) — a brand-new listing can
     pin a codebase years old and long since audited. Faster first pass: the repo
     object's `created_at`/`pushed_at`, plus any in-repo release manifest
     (`VERSIONS`, RELEASES.md) mapping version -> commit -> first-distribution
     date; that dates the code without needing the pinned sha. When the code IS
     fresh, enter through the component named in the newest release-prep commit —
     it is the least-audited part of an otherwise heavily audited protocol.
   - release commits named "deploy X" or "setup X market" usually touch only
     deployment JSONs, OpenZeppelin manifests and config, not `.sol` sources.
     List the files each commit actually changed before scoring a target as fresh
     code; the file-list commands and the rule live in `bugbounty-target-selection`,
     section "Commit messages are not proof of new code surface".
   - on-chain scope: `https://<chain>.blockscout.com/api/v2/addresses/<addr>` ->
     `creation_transaction_hash` -> that tx's `timestamp` = the real deployment
     date; a fresh listing can point at year-old contracts.
   - **Confirm the feature is live on an in-scope address before staking.** A
     release commit can add a feature to repo HEAD while every target in scope
     still runs an older version. Batch `eth_call` to the version getter on every
     scope address (`apiVersion()` for Yearn-style vaults, selector `0x25829410`)
     and to a getter that exists only in the new version. Include addresses the
     program folds in via an "all contracts listed on <site>" clause, not just
     the visible asset table. If none report the new version, park the idea: a
     bug in undeployed code cannot reach the assets the bounty covers.
     For a diamond/proxy, explorer verification can lag the live facet set. Enumerate
     `facetAddresses()` and call a feature-only getter on the diamond; a non-zero
     answer proves the upgrade is live even when the explorer's verified `System.sol`
     still lacks the new fields. Do not park the target from stale verified source
     alone.
   - **A component can be explicitly full scope and still be Testnet only while the
     reward is tied to Mainnet code.** Before committing a day to the least-audited
     module, read the program's deployment clause and inventory the same release's
     Mainnet commits by changed-file list. Rank by payable surface, not by code
     freshness. A clean verdict on a Testnet-only component is not closure of the
     release; the unswept Mainnet modules are the carry-over that must be named.
   - On Solana, source presence is NOT dispatch presence. A handler file, its
     snake_case name in the ELF string pool, and one of its log phrases can all exist
     while the instruction is absent from the deployed dispatcher. Before investing in
     a PoC, check the CamelCase `<Name>Instruction` dispatch string, the official SDK
     IDL's `instructions[]`, and finally call it with `sha256("global:<snake_case>")[:8]`;
     `Custom(101) InstructionFallbackNotFound` means the discriminator missed, NOT that
     the handler is absent. Derive the exact snake_case name from the `pub fn` in `lib.rs`
     and from the SDK IDL's camelCase name before killing a lead. Real case: a handler
     file named `handler_repay_and_withdraw_redeem.rs` dispatches as
     `repay_and_withdraw_and_redeem` (IDL `repayAndWithdrawAndRedeem`); a PoC using
     `global:repay_and_withdraw_redeem` returned 101 for both arms and was wrongly
     recorded as source-only until the correct discriminator dispatched it on deployed
     bytecode. Only after both names agree does a 101 justify a kill in the coverage
     ledger. Why: source-only code cannot move bounty assets, but a wrong discriminator
     can fake that conclusion.
   - After the discriminator matches, verify the account list against a REAL successful
     transaction for that instruction before trusting any ProgramTest constraint error.
     Enumerate recent signatures for the program, fetch candidates with JSON encoding,
     decode instruction data as base58 (not base64), keep a tx whose first eight bytes equal
     the discriminator, and compare its account count and order with the SDK IDL's flattened
     account list. A cached meta file with a different discriminator or fewer accounts is a
     different instruction; its `InvalidProgramId` or `AccountNotEnoughKeys` result is harness
     debt, not protocol behaviour. Why: a wrong account list reproduces the program's own
     constraint failures faithfully and manufactures a false verdict.
   - cost: platforms charge per-report deposits (Sherlock USDC 250, Cantina 50,
     HackenProof 5). Cantina refunds for valid AND legitimately invalid reports;
     only spam, low-effort/AI content or inflated severity slashes the deposit,
     per its deposits doc. Factor that into expected value and never book a
     refundable deposit as a sunk fee.
   - contest reality check: before investing in a contest found via search,
     confirm the page is a PRODUCTION listing, not a demo/preview. Demo pages say
     so explicitly and carry contradictory dates; a preview subdomain plus
     inconsistent start/end dates is a hard stop. Confirm a named judge and an
     actual funding guarantee. A contest advertised as POST-AUDIT with a
     Critical-only, large-loss threshold is not an unaudited fresh surface,
     however new the listing looks.
   - payout reality check: the reward must be liquid money with a stated amount
     and conversion. Points / airdrop credits with an unspecified conversion are
     not a payable target, however fresh and unaudited the code is.
   If every fresh-looking listing is old code, the fresh SURFACE is the DIFF
   between the pinned commits (see the signature-refactor rule under step 3), or
   the next audit competition — pre-launch code is the only reliably fresh scope.
2. **Recon** — map every new entry point, its caller permission, the state it
   touches, the events it emits, and its integrations (token, oracle, bridge,
   admin, fee, pause).
3. **Consistency** — the core pass. For each action: ownership, permission,
   accounting, rounding/precision, idempotency/replay, reentrancy, slippage,
   rate limit, pause, admin, storage layout, error handling, event completeness.
   **Signature-layer refactors are a forgery seam:** when a release moves or
   rewrites the code that verifies signed payloads, extract every
   `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(...))` argument list from the old and the new
   source and diff them field by field — any field the new hash dropped is now
   attacker-controllable (forgery). Identical field lists clear the whole
   refactor in minutes. Read the OLD file raw at
   `raw.githubusercontent.com/<org>/<repo>/<sha>/<path>` and the per-file
   patches at `api.github.com/repos/<org>/<repo>/compare/<shaA>...<shaB>`
   (unauthenticated) — no need to clone both trees.
4. **Impact filter** — keep only candidates that mean loss of funds: double
   claim, withdraw over balance, mint without backing, wrong interest/fee,
   stale/manipulated oracle, stuck funds, privilege escalation.
5. **PoC** — reproduce on testnet/fork; show state before -> action -> state
   after; prove value moved or got locked; check the program's grading clauses
   and that it is not a duplicate.
   - When a hand-written minimal interface call reverts with empty `0x` data,
     diff that function's signature against the source before treating it as
     on-chain behaviour: multi-argument view functions are commonly encoded as
     single-argument ones. Why: the wrong selector hits no function and reverts
     with empty data, which reads like a protocol failure and starts a false lead.
   - Confirm the function selector is actually installed on the mock diamond before trusting negative tests. If the harness deploys only a subset of facets, every invalid-input case can pass with `Diamond: Function does not exist` while the real validation is never exercised. Add the missing facet with the protocol's own diamond-cut helper, then rerun.
   - Seed arbitrary state with the protocol's mock facets instead of forcing the production deposit path when the mock invariant blocks setup. Record the happy path as unverified if the mock still reverts; do not claim a valid flow from negative tests alone. Why: a harness that only proves reverts cannot establish that the feature works.
   - Before rebuilding a stateful setup in Foundry, check whether the repo ships a Hardhat suite that already configures it (recapitalization, governance, oracle, Barn Raise). Run that suite first and add the new split to it. Why: a Foundry mock harness can hit harness-only invariant or zero-denominator failures even when the protocol path is sound; the native suite's fixture proves both the baseline and the new case.
   - When enumerating holders from event logs on a public RPC, chunk the block
     range to the provider cap (publicnode Base rejects ranges over 50k blocks)
     and dedupe addresses across chunks. Why: one wide range errors and looks
     like "no holders", which can kill a live lead.
6. **Report** — title with feature + impact, numbered repro, tx hash + PoC,
   quantified impact, fix recommendation, severity per the program's rubric.

## Speed

The window is short: aim to report within 1-7 days of release. A 15-minute
pass per release (find the new surface -> ask the consistency question -> test
one seam on a fork) is enough to decide whether to invest.

## Checklist

The full checklist, including the 15-minute version and the consistency
questions, is in [references/checklist.md](references/checklist.md).

For Solana PoCs rebuilt from live transactions, the harness reconstruction
recipe is in [references/solana-poc-from-live-tx.md](references/solana-poc-from-live-tx.md).

### bugbounty-target-selection

*Sumber: `installed` - `skills/02-recon-targeting/bugbounty-target-selection/SKILL.md`*

> Use when picking a bug-bounty target: verify rep gate.

# Bug-Bounty Target Selection

Choosing WHERE to hunt matters more than hunting harder. A third-party list or
PDF draws you to a target; verify it on the platform BEFORE investing days.

## When to Use

Load this before starting work on any bug-bounty target, and whenever you are
tempted to invest in a program drawn from a list, PDF, or aggregator. Use it to
check the reputation gate, scope accessibility, and audit depth FIRST, so you
don't sink days into a target you cannot submit to or that is already audited.

## Start from the workspace's own work ledger

Check `references/campaign-ledger.md` first for targets already driven to a
verified negative, then confirm the on-disk artifacts still exist. Before
cloning or scouting any target, list `<audit-root>/<target>/` for a
`VERDICT*` or `*TRACE*.md` note, prior repo checkouts and PoC/harness files. A
parked verdict backed by invariant traces is a completed engagement: report it
instead of re-cloning or repeating the same campaign, and clean up any duplicate
checkout you created. If resuming that work, re-read the current program page
before relying on the old verdict — gates such as KYC can change after it was
written.

When asked which targets from a list have NOT been worked on, never answer from
recollection. Scan the Hermes session DB read-only, then corroborate with the
audit tree:

```python
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect('file:C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/hermes/state.db?mode=ro', uri=True)
rows = c.execute('select m.session_id, m.role, m.content from messages m').fetchall()
# per target: case-insensitive aliases -> hit count, distinct sessions, sample user turns
```

Exclude the current session id from the DB scan before counting hits. The user's own list or question injects every target name into this session, so including it inflates every target to a recent hit and hides the real history. Identify the current session from the conversation's own messages, then group the remaining hits by session and role before corroborating with artifacts.

Follow with an inventory of the audit workspace (`E:/audit` on this host): a
cloned repo plus a PoC, harness or verdict note means the target was really
worked; one or two mentions inside a research PDF or an aggregator post mean
it was only scouted. Report the two buckets separately and name the artifact
that justifies each classification.

Use program-specific phrases when scanning, not bare brand words. Short or
common names generate substring false positives (`raac` inside an unrelated
Android class name, `exactly` as ordinary English), so corroborate every hit
with an artifact path before calling a target worked on.

## Query public report corpora before choosing a target

A disclosed-report corpus such as POJIA (https://cve.pojia.ai) is a fast
pre-filter for which bug classes and weaknesses have actually paid in a
program. Query it for discovery paths before scouting code, then apply the
gates below. The REST/MCP recipe, verification caveats and the live-stats
check live in `references/public-report-corpora.md`.

Treat the corpus as a lead source, not evidence. Annotations can be
model-generated and most corpora serve excerpts plus links, so open the
original report and carry the pattern forward only as a hypothesis. Verify the
corpus's own live stats endpoint instead of repeating counts from the post that
advertised it.

## Compare a long list on toolchain fit

When the ask is a comparison rather than a single pick, rank on four columns:
fit with the tools actually installed, gate and fee to submit, freshness versus
competition, and whether the payout mechanic pays the impact the operator cares
about. Put the per-row caveat beside the score: audit depth, KYC at payout,
submission fee, known-issues exclusions, mainnet-testing bans. Deliver the
matrix in chat plus one durable markdown file, then numbered next-step options.
When the operator answers that menu with several numbers or letters, execute every
selected item to completion in the same turn before replying, in the order given.
Write the deliverable in casual Indonesian without em-dash. Before delivering ANY
Indonesian artifact (comparison matrix, verdict, ledger note or result file),
grep the file for non-Latin characters, doubled words and leaked template or
placeholder syntax: generated Indonesian reports can leak stray CJK/Japanese
glyphs, duplicated tokens and leftover `${...}` fragments, and a broken
character in a reward figure or path makes the report look unreliable.

When the platform exposes its own list API, rank from that data instead of the
rendered cards. Derive `findings / days live` as a competition-saturation proxy,
then combine with freshness, pot size and the severity tiers that actually pay;
aggregate reward tiers over all in-scope asset groups. Present the score with the
caveat that a low finding rate can mean a hard or non-paying scope, not an open
field. Cantina's endpoint and the streamed-payload field map are in
`references/program-recon-and-fork-tests.md`.

## Read the in-scope surface type and AI clauses before ranking

Open the in-scope asset groups, not just the pot: a top-paying program can list
only website / web-app / API assets, which disqualifies a Solidity-only operator
regardless of reward size. Read each asset group's `outOfScope` flag and its
asset names/descriptions, then match the surface to the operator's toolchain
before scoring. Why: a large pot on a web-only scope wastes the whole deep-dive
budget.

Check the program rules for AI/automation eligibility clauses. Some programs
state that unverified AI-forwarded reports are spam, that the fee is forfeited
for them, that AI assistance must be disclosed, and that a finding without human
review is ineligible. Treat that as a fee-risk gate: keep PoCs local, verify every
function, address, code path and exploit step against deployed code, and require
human review before any submission. Why: the fee is non-refundable on those
programs, so an agent-drafted report can cost money and pay nothing.

Use an aggregator's one-line program metadata (rep requirement, PoC flag,
submission fee, submission count, total rewards) as a FAST PRE-FILTER across a
long list, then open the official program pages for the finalists. Aggregator
metadata is a bucket, never the last word: some slugs 404 or omit the gate, so
an absent field means unknown, not zero. On Immunefi the program JSON `features`
can expose `Pay to Submit` and `Pay to Mediate - No Free Mediations` even when the
public page shows no fee: quote exact aggregator amounts as caveats, not facts,
and treat no-free-mediation as an extra dispute cost. The same JSON carries an
`audits` array and `pocPerTypeAndSeverity`; use their counts as a fast
audit-depth and PoC-burden prefilter before opening every finalist page.
For the full Immunefi program list in one fetch, the HackenProof public
program-list filter recipe, escaped JSON snapshots on other platform pages, and
the deployed-contract fork-test recipe, see
`references/program-recon-and-fork-tests.md`.

## Verify the reputation gate on the PROGRAM PAGE, not a list

Third-party lists and PDFs publish stale/optimistic reputation requirements.
Always open the program page and read the real "Reputation N points required".
Verified example (Nov 2026, HackenProof) vs what the list claimed:

| Program | Real rep | List claimed |
|---|---|---|
| RedStone | 150 | ">50" |
| GMGN, Starknet Web&SC/Staking, XT, Gate US, Turbos, NAVI | 100 | ">50" |
| Rhea, Arcadia, WhiteBIT | 50 | "11-50" |

Your rep must be >= the requirement to submit. A missed gate = zero payout for
the whole engagement. Factor rep INTO target choice, not after.

Read the gate from raw HTML when the reader drops it: a Jina-rendered program
page can carry the full policy yet omit the sidebar requirement chips
(Reputation, identity, paid-report rules). Fetch the page directly and grep the
`<dt>...</dt><dd>...</dd>` pairs, for example the `<dt>Reputation</dt>` chip
followed by `50 points required`. Why: a gate absent from rendered text means
unknown, not "no gate", and it decides eligibility before any code work.

On HackenProof the same raw HTML carries a devalue-encoded Nuxt payload whose
fields are integer indices into a flat array; decode it to recover
`minReputation`, `kycRequired`, `pocRequired`, `submissionFee`, `maxReward`,
`startDate`, `endDate` and `repoLink` when the reader drops those chips. Recipe: in the opportunity-vetting skill's bounty-program-verification.md,
section "HackenProof program pages".

Treat a platform's KYC filter as a fast prefilter only, never as proof the
scope is open. A program can pass `kyc=false` while its Program Rules require
KYC plus at least one paid Medium-or-higher report to unlock the code. Grep the
finalist page text for `KYC`, `paid report`, `access to the code` and
`permission` before ranking it. Why: structured filter chips encode metadata,
while scope-access conditions live in free-text rules and can block every
submission until satisfied.

## Find the right program, and read what the reward mechanic rewards

- Program slugs follow the *program*, not the protocol: `<platform>/programs/<protocol>` is often a 404 because the deployment sits inside an umbrella program named after the chain or ecosystem. Search by chain/ecosystem name, then expand the scope table ("Show all targets") and read any **Additional Scope** clause — it frequently extends coverage to the docs' address-book link listing ALL production deployments, so the visible core list is only a subset.
- A retired paid bounty remains in aggregator lists and X roundups long after
  it stops paying. Read the program's own doc for "ended / no longer pays" and
  the platform changelog for paused or removed status before ranking an entry
  as available. A closed program with a referral tail is not a bounty.
- A reopen announcement is a lead, not a green light. Verify live status on the
  platform and confirm with a submission timestamp after the reopen; if the
  scope is hidden behind an application, park the target until approved rather
  than scouting blind.
- Read the reward mechanic as a hunting hint. A program defining the damage baseline in a specific way — e.g. "maximum reward = 10% of funds directly affected, calculated from the circuit breaker's maximum withdrawal limit; if the bug BYPASSES the circuit breaker, funds affected equals the TVL" — is telling you which bug class pays: anything that moves value out while skipping the rate limiter. Definitions like "significant freezing of funds for >1 year" also pay; read them as target classes, not fine print.
- Read the known-issues list before hunting (usually an `<org>/security` repo, e.g. `KNOWN_ISSUES.md`): your intended surface being absent from it is a reason to invest, and the *neighbourhood* of a disclosed issue is where variants live. The list often lives ON the platform page itself (e.g. Sherlock's "Previous Audits" section), scrape it there even if the linked repo 404s (private). When the program links audit PDFs as known issues, also read each report's conclusion and its paragraph about issues noticed outside audit scope: acknowledged residuals and out-of-scope observations are rejection-prone, so a report built on one must add a runnable, unprivileged exploit with quantified loss, not restate the auditor's note.
- Read the program's GRADING CLAUSES before deep work and pre-classify your candidate finding classes against them. The trusted-roles clause ("privileged roles are fully trusted... if any privileged role can harm the protocol or the users in any way, it's considered informational") zeroes out entire classes: admin-set oracles/NAV feeds, dormant admin-gated powers (bypass/lock functions), trusted-forwarder bypasses. Check each candidate: can a NON-privileged actor trigger it? If not, it is informational — do not invest or stake on it. For a live role-gated entry point, read the on-chain authority before deep work (Solmate-style `canCall(address(0), target, selector)` plus a couple of random EOAs). If every EOA is denied, a bug inside an admin/decoder component cannot pay by itself: the report must show that an unprivileged address GAINS that capability. Do not spend a stake on a component whose only gate cannot be crossed.
- When the platform program page and the project's own docs disagree on reward
  tiers or submission channel, treat the platform page (the escrow holder) as
  authoritative for submission and do not switch to the project's email until
  the discrepancy is resolved: an email route bypasses the escrow that made the
  target worth selecting in the first place. Record both versions with their
  modification dates and ask for written confirmation.
- Treat the program's own address book as a LOOKUP, not as scope, when the terms say so: a registry page can list retired, shut-down and migrated products beside live ones. Select contracts from the named live-product scope and confirm each candidate's production status before mapping its money flow.
- Fork-only evidence clauses pre-kill whole report classes. When the terms demand a fork of the deployed implementation at a recent block, a PoC on mocks, a local redeploy, or storage patched over a production address is invalid. Check also for a named on-chain victim, a control run without the bug, and a ban on impersonating governance or keepers to manufacture the condition, then price the extra fork work before committing.
- A minimum demonstrated-loss floor plus a percentage-of-loss cap (payouts only above a stated USD amount, capped at a fraction of loss, with no Medium/Low tiers) means the reward formula decides eligibility, not the severity label. Compute the funds at risk needed to clear the floor before choosing a bug class.
- Separate the platform from the payer. A platform-hosted program can still pay directly from the protocol in its own token while the platform only triages and mediates; escrow protection and payout liquidity are then different from a platform-paid bounty. Quote the token, chain and payer before ranking. Why: a large USD maximum in a volatile project token is not the same exposure as a stablecoin escrow.
- Price the submission against the plausible payout: Sherlock stake (~$250/report, refunded if valid), Cantina deposits that are refunded for valid AND legitimately invalid reports (slashed only for spam, low-effort/AI content or inflated severity, see `docs.cantina.security/researchers/participation/deposits`), against floors like the platforms' own minimum for a valid Critical. Look for "Deposit required" on the bounty page and never record a refundable deposit as a sunk fee.
- Compare the percentage-of-funds mechanic and the funds-at-risk needed to hit the cap, not only the advertised maximum: a 20% mechanic halves the required damage versus 10%, which changes which bug classes justify deep work.
- Economics + life-signs pre-check (deployment TVL vs payout mechanic; frontend banner/news) before any deep work — worked numbers and the full method live in the **evm-bounty-source-audit** skill's economics reference.

## Immunefi scope pages hide most in-scope instances

The visible asset table is only the core list. Click the `Show all` button and
extract every `a[href*="etherscan.io/address/"]`, dedupe by address, and walk up
to the card containing `Name` and `Added on`. The `Added on` dates reveal which
contracts came from the latest release. Then open the protocol's own
address-registry repo (`maple-labs/address-registry`, `address-registry.json` is
a good pattern): the program's \"all instances deployed from all factories\"
clause makes those live proxy instances in-scope even when absent from the 40-row
table. Verify new entries with `eth_getCode` on a public RPC
(`https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com` works when hosted RPCs return 403).

For EVM view calls without web3, compute selectors with
`Crypto.Hash.keccak(digest_bits=256)` and batch `eth_call` on publicnode. The
correct `totalAssets()` selector is `0x01e1d114`; do not rely on memorised
selectors. Comparing pool `totalAssets()` and strategy `assetsUnderManagement()`
separates funded instances from bootstrap-only (1 unit) deployments before
choosing where to hunt. For scopes with dozens of addresses across many chains,
use `references/multichain-scope-recon.md` to normalise the list and rank by TVL.

When a view returns a struct, ABI encoding gives EVERY field its own 32-byte word
regardless of how the struct is packed in storage. Read the field order from the
repo's deployment artifact (`deployments/<chain>/<Name>.json` in Hardhat/Foundry
projects) and decode one word per field, in order. Applying storage-packing
arithmetic to the returned hex produces plausible but wrong values, for example
a boolean flag read as false when it is true. Prefer those deployment artifacts
over explorer verified-source APIs when the explorer is gated: they carry the
proxy address, implementation address, constructor args and the full ABI.

## Fuzzing a funded instance: harness pattern that works here

Medusa accepts property functions WITH arguments; Echidna property mode does
not (`Test "..." has arguments, aborting`). Build two harnesses over the same
setup: a Medusa harness with `echidna_*()` entry points that take random args
and wrap risky calls in low-level `call`/`try` so expected reverts are not
counted as property failures, and an Echidna harness in `--test-mode assertion`
whose `fuzz*()` entry points end with `assert(invariant)`. Put privileged
entry points behind a small actor contract registered through the protocol's
own Globals/registry so no VM prank cheatcode is needed.

crytic-compile (used by both Medusa and Echidna) spawns `forge` from PATH. The
`~/bin` shim makes bare `forge` Foundry here; still assert `forge --version`
starts with `forge Version:` before a fuzz run, because a `manifest.yml` line
means the Atlassian CLI answered and compilation will fail.

## Commit messages are not proof of new code surface

A release message like "deploy X", "setup X market" or "upgrade auditor" usually
means deployment JSONs, OpenZeppelin manifest entries and config changes, not a
new `.sol` implementation. Before scoring a target as fresh code, list the files
each recent commit touched and check the source file's own history:

```bash
gh api --jq '.files[] | [.filename, .status] | @tsv' \
  "repos/<org>/<repo>/commits/<sha>"
gh api --jq '.[0] | [.commit.author.date, .sha[0:10], .commit.message] | @tsv' \
  "repos/<org>/<repo>/commits?path=contracts/<File>.sol&per_page=1"
```

Why: deploying existing code changes deployment artifacts on every release, so a
message-only freshness check turns a plain new listing into a false "unaudited
new code" claim. Newly deployed instances can still be a real edge, but classify
them as deployed-config surface, not unaudited source.

## Before claiming an area is unaudited, match hashes

Audit PDFs usually list a repo commit and per-file SHA256. Recompute those
hashes with `git show <commit>:<path> | sha256sum` before assuming coverage.
Then diff the audited file against the verified deployed source: a handful of
cosmetic lines (interface removed, public→external) still counts as direct
coverage. Also check the live authority: `getRolesWithCapability(target, selector)`
and `isCapabilityPublic(target, selector)` can show a whole component is
decommissioned (all capabilities revoked), which ends the hunt faster than
source review alone.

## Verify deployed source before trusting repo HEAD

Blockscout's API v2 (`https://<chain>.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/<address>`)
returns verified `source_code`, `additional_sources`, compiler version, EVM
version, and `is_changed_bytecode` without an API key. On Etherscan-only chains
use `api.<domain>/api?module=contract&action=getsourcecode&address=...`.
Etherscan V2 uses the unified endpoint with `chainid` and `apikey` instead. Multi-file `SourceCode` arrives as a JSON string wrapped in one extra brace pair: strip the first and last character before `json.loads`, then read `sources`. Compare main contract files by basename; dependency files under `node_modules` show as missing if the local index excluded them, so a raw missing-file count is not evidence of a source mismatch.
Compare each returned file against repo HEAD after stripping comments and
whitespace. A repo can be far ahead of what is live: a Veda vault's decoder had
0/27 matching files (deployed version rejected compose messages and SVM CCIP;
HEAD supported both). Auditing HEAD then gives false confidence. `is_changed_bytecode=false`
only means bytecode was not changed after verification, not that repo HEAD is
the deployed version. When many files differ, compare the economic formulas
rather than the file count: a rename plus helper extraction can be a large diff
with identical fee math. For sanitizer/decoder code, a scan for unused `address`
parameters is not sufficient; separately scan address-typed fields inside
struct/bytes arguments and confirm each reaches the packed output.

If live bytecode differs in size from the locally compiled artifact, do not
report a source mismatch yet: read distinctive view functions and immutable
constants (`name()`, `symbol()`, `cap()`, fixed fee bps, role and lock getters)
with `eth_call` and compare them with the pinned source. Why: optimizer and
via-IR settings change deployed bytecode while leaving public state and logic
identical, so selector-level agreement is the cheaper provenance check.

## Bytes32 address halves in sanitizer outputs are left-aligned

When a decoder splits a `bytes32` recipient into two `address` halves via
`address(bytes20(bytes16(x)))` and `address(bytes20(bytes16(x << 128)))`,
the resulting address contains the 16 source bytes as its HIGH bytes with four
zero bytes appended. A test that constructs the `bytes32` by right-aligning an
`address` (`bytes32(uint256(uint160(a)))`) puts the value in the low bytes and
will see zeros in the first half. Left-align with `bytes32(uint256(uint160(a)) << 96)`
or assert against `address(bytes20(bytes16(original)))` instead of the raw
address.

## Mainnet-fork invariant suites need an archive RPC

Stateful invariant tests pinned to an old block fail on publicnode with
"Archive requests require a personal token". `https://eth-mainnet.public.blastapi.io`
answered archive `eth_getBalance` at block 25,523,119 without a key and ran the
suite to completion. Budget time: a 2-pool modular-strategy invariant run took
~400 seconds. Verify archive access with a single `eth_getBalance` at the pinned
block before launching the full campaign.

Event-log recon has per-RPC range caps that vary wildly: `https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc`
accepted a 2,000,000-block `eth_getLogs` window, while blastapi caps it at 10 blocks,
dRPC at 100, and Tenderly at 1,000; publicnode demands an archive token. Parallelise
wide scans with a thread pool and chunk to each provider's real cap. Etherscan V1
`module=logs` endpoints now return a deprecation notice; use V2.

For explorer logs, Blockscout v2 exposes
`/api/v2/addresses/<address>/logs?topic=<topic0>` with pagination via
`next_page_params` (`block_number`, `index`, `items_count`). Direct `urllib` fetches
can get 403 while the explorer HTML loads; retry with `curl -A 'Mozilla/5.0'
-H 'Referer: <explorer origin>'` or extract the address page through a text reader.
`base.blockscout.com` may 403 while `explorer.base.org` serves HTML, not the v2 API.
When a factory event names a proxy, read state from the proxy: SDK manifest
addresses are frequently uninitialized implementations returning zeros.

When a test helper creates a new pool it may overwrite an inherited
`poolManager` state variable (Maple's `_createPoolSharingStrategy` does). Cache
the original pool manager address before creating the second pool, or the
"other pool" assertions silently test the same pool twice.

## Before trusting an audit report, diff its final commit against HEAD

Published audit PDFs pin an audited commit and a final commit. Clone the repo
and run `git diff -w <audit-final> HEAD -- contracts`: formatting-only diffs
mean the report still applies; semantic diffs are fixes that landed after the
review (often the audit's own recommendations) or unaudited new logic. Name
exactly which findings were fixed before calling a surface "still open".

For Foundry repos on this host, bare `forge` is Foundry through the `~/bin`
shim; if it ever prints `15.1.0` or writes `manifest.yml`, the Atlassian CLI
answered: call `C:/Users/TUF-GAMING/.foundry/bin/forge.exe` directly. For repos
that omit `foundry.toml` and vendor libraries, clone the exact tagged
dependencies named in the repo or audit into `lib/` with git
(`git clone --depth 1 --branch <tag> <repo> lib/<dir>`) and write remappings for
`forge-std/` and `@openzeppelin/contracts/`. Set `via_ir = true` with the
optimizer when legacy tests hit stack-too-deep. Run `forge test --match-path
<file>` for the PoC after a baseline run: missing docs/config fixtures can fail
unrelated tests for filesystem reasons, which is not a finding. Maple-style repos use `modules/`
with git@github.com submodules: init with
`git -c url."https://github.com/".insteadOf=git@github.com: submodule update --init --recursive`
or compilation fails on missing imports. Run `forge test -q` as a baseline
before any PoC work. If `forge build` fails inside `script/` on stale helper
signatures, do not treat it as a blocker: `forge test --match-path <file>`
compiles src + test but not scripts and usually still runs. For an oversized
submodule, shallow clone with `--filter=blob:none --sparse` then
`git sparse-checkout set` only the directories the imports need.

## Verify audit depth from the repo before investing

Some repos ship per-deployment component-level audit gaps (for example
`deployments/addresses/<chain>/*.json` with `contractMetadata[*].auditGap`).
Aggregate the gap values across deployments and cross-reference components
marked `unaudited` or `state,selectors,auth` against the INSTANCES THAT HOLD
FUNDS. This is how fresh surfaces are found inside a codebase that looks
uniformly well-audited at the top level.

"Well-audited" = the repo ships audit PDFs or the protocol names established
firms (OtterSec, MoveBit, Veridise, Asymptotic, Trail of Bits, Sherlock, Hacken,
Zellic, CertiK, BlockSec) or has formal verification. Well-audited ~= verified
negatives. Check `find -iname '*audit*.pdf'`, an `/audits` docs page, a Security
section. Also read the program page's own audit statement: it may say the base
contracts are audited while the actual in-scope deployments are not. Treat
that as a claim, not a finding: pull the deployed source (Etherscan HTML
`data-csource`, Blockscout v2, or Sourcify) and byte-diff it against the repo
commit named in the audit PDF after stripping whitespace. A byte-match means
the code IS covered and kills the fresh-listing thesis; only a genuine diff
opens the hunt. Sui/Move protocols are
routinely audited (MoveBit/OtterSec/Veridise) - assume audited unless the repo
is fresh. Prefer fresh/less-audited: recently deployed V2s, new protocols, small
TVL, code the audits did not cover.

## Self-hosted / non-platform bounty programs

When a program uses its own landing page and form instead of Immunefi /
HackerOne / Sherlock / Cantina, there is no platform escrow, no published
payout history and no platform-enforced severity contract. Vet before deep
work:

- A severity guide saying "Critical = loss or theft of funds" is a
  CLASSIFICATION, not a payout promise. Search the launch thread, landing
  page, poster images and the form for an actual reward table or payout
  terms. If none exists anywhere, label it "no reward published" and do not
  imply it pays. Matching the user's loss-of-funds-only criterion is not
  enough when the payment commitment itself is missing.
- Verify the operating entity, not just the brand: WHOIS the old and new
  domains separately (a young product domain on a decades-old brand domain
  is normal, not proof of legitimacy), the parent's own press releases,
  company registries, and the site's Terms for regulator disclaimers. A
  public-company parent confirmed in a press release is a real signal. A
  "scam / withdrawal issues" write-up is not evidence until its BODY is read:
  such pages often just list transparency gaps (no SEC/FinCEN record,
  address mismatch, low traffic).
- Check what the report form costs the hunter: fields demanding a wallet
  address, handles and email mean personal data goes to whoever hosts that
  form, which may be a third-party CRM.

## Platform landscape (rep gates are HackenProof-specific)

- **HackenProof**: rep gates 50/100/150; curated (well-audited); scopes often
  KYC- or paid-report-gated (`hackenproof-public/*`).
- **Immunefi**: ~150 programs, NO reputation gate; KYC per program, PoC
  required, loss-of-funds focus. Breaks the rep deadlock.
- **Intigriti**: no reputation gate, but many programs are application gated:
  scope and policy stay hidden until approval, and the public programs API's
  `status`/`confidentialityLevel` is the live signal. ID verification is now
  required at submission creation for reward-eligible programs, not just at
  payout. Verify both before scouting code; recipe in the opportunity-vetting
  skill's bounty-program-verification reference.
- **Mantis**: no reputation gate, platform escrow, and orgs are marked
  `verified` by Mantis staff. Its published set can be very small, so enumerate
  every published/verified bounty instead of trusting aggregator lists; newer
  programs often carry precise loss-floor and fork-PoC grading clauses. Full
  API and field-name recipe lives in the opportunity-vetting skill, in its
  bounty-program-verification reference file.
- **Cantina**: ~47 programs, optional per-program deposit (commonly $50, refundable except spam/AI/inflated severity), KYC at join or at payout depending on the program. **Sherlock**: ~38,
  $250 stake. **Code4rena shut down (2026)**. Check Sherlock's `/contests` and
  `/bug-bounties` separately: contests can be empty while staked bug bounties
  are still live.
- Rep-gated out of good HackenProof targets -> pivot to a no-gate platform
  instead of grinding low-rep web2 for rep points.

## Reality check: "less audited" rarely coexists with "SC + high reward"

High-reward SC programs ARE the well-audited ones. In the rep<=100 band the
genuinely less-audited targets are web2/apps or small/zero-payout. If a target
seems to be all of {less-audited, SC, high-reward, accessible}, re-check - one
of those is usually false.

## Fresh code when every program is audited: hunt a competition

Competitions put NOT-yet-deployed code in scope for a fixed window - the only
target class that is genuinely less-audited, and a level playing field (first
valid finder wins; no reputation gate).

Discovery: `bbradar.io/contests` (calendar across platforms - check "live now"
first), `cantina.xyz/opportunities/competitions`, the Immunefi site's
audit-competition section, `codehawks.cyfrin.io`.

Mechanics to read off the competition page before investing:
- The pool is set by the highest valid severity and shared among all valid
  finders (e.g. Critical->$250k, High->$125k, Medium->$70k, Low->$30k), not
  paid per finder.
- A runnable PoC is required for EVERY report (no PoC = closed); KYC is
  required for payout; mid-contest fixes are often allowed.
- Read the PoC environment clause: if it demands a local devnet / real binaries,
  the slice matching your tooling (e.g. a Foundry test for the Solidity
  contracts) is the tractable part; the rest is heavy node/firmware work.
- Read the scope off the competition page's own Scope tab (Immunefi:
  `/audit-competition/<slug>/scope/`) - it pins the exact commit per repo and
  names the accepted PoC environments per component.
- Weigh difficulty BEFORE investing: a competition on a major chain's own core
  protocol draws hundreds of researchers plus tier-1 firms and the code is
  already audited many times over - a long shot for a solo hunter. Time-box one
  focused pass over the slice matching your tooling, then park it; smaller/newer
  protocols are where the field is thinner.

## Target vetting checklist (run before deep work)

1. Rep requirement on the program page <= my rep?
2. Scope accessible (not application-gated with hidden scope, KYC, or
   >=1-paid-report gated)?
3. Audit depth (repo PDFs / named firms)?
4. Payout history ($ paid > 0; $0 = unproven)?
5. Submission count and its delta between snapshots (a count climbing several reports per day means the easy surface is already picked over)?
6. Language matches my tooling? Verify from the program page's language tags AND the repo's file extension (.sol / .rs / .clar / .move / .cairo) - a protocol's name or an aggregator label can mislead (a "Solana LST" from the list was actually Clarity/Stacks). Run `gh api repos/<o>/<r>/languages` as well: a nominally Solidity repo can hide a large Vyper core that needs a separate compiler. Confirm the compiler and test runner before ranking the target: Cairo needs `scarb` plus a Starknet test runner, Substrate runtime work needs the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` rustup target, and Clarity needs its own toolchain. When one is absent, park with the named install and source-unlock conditions instead of reading source you cannot turn into a PoC.
7. Known issues / disclosed hacks excluded from scope? Read the list itself (a `security` repo, `KNOWN_ISSUES.md`), not just the fact that one exists.
8. Submission cost (stake/fee) priced against the plausible payout?

9. Grading clauses (trusted roles / severity formula / known-issues content) extracted and applied to your candidate classes?
10. For an on-chain target, every deployed address validated with `chain-scope-guard` against a transcribed program scope file, including the Additional Scope address book?
11. Public report corpus checked for the candidate class/program, discovery paths read, and annotations verified against the original report?
12. Every finalist scope asset confirmed DEPLOYED, not merely audited? An asset
    pinned to a private dev repo and absent from the first-party deployment
    manifests is a "Latest audited" item and cannot carry a fork PoC yet.
13. In-scope asset types match my toolchain (SC vs web/API), and the rules checked
    for AI/automation clauses, disclosure duties and fee-forfeiture terms?

Skip the target if (1) or (2) fails, or if (3) says well-audited AND (4) says $0.

## Verified-negative is a real outcome

Well-audited targets yield verified negatives (observed: 5 surfaces on one EVM
lending core, an LST, all clean). Record the negative, note the remaining
untested edge, and move on - do not keep grinding a target whose audits already
cover the code. The edge, if any, is the fresh / deployed-config surface, not
the audited library.

For an audit contest with a public prior audit report, transcribe its finding
table and map each candidate PoC to an accepted finding or a privileged-role
path before submitting. A runnable PoC that only reproduces an accepted finding
is a verified negative, not a payable report. Why: contest rules exclude known
issues and rogue privileged roles, so the technically correct exploit is ground
the program refuses to pay.

Time-box the DEEP phase: extract the grading clauses + map the money surface
FIRST (a few hours); if the clauses pre-kill your candidate classes and the
style is uniformly guarded (constructor/argument checks, Ceil/Floor rounding
conservatism, per-order limits, post-action HF sweeps), park after the
surface-map sweep instead of line-reading every seam. 30+ deep reads to zero
payable is a signal to stop, not to push harder; leave a findings ledger +
an upgrade watch (proxy impl-slot + public address-book hash on a cron) so new
deployments re-open the hunt cheaply.

## Post-hack rebuilds: the known hack is OUT of scope

A program launched after a hack targets the REBUILT code; the disclosed exploit
is excluded. The value is whether the fix is complete / has variants and whether
other logic is sound - not re-finding the public bug. The rebuilt repo is often
KYC-gated; the public upstream mirror is the pre-hack version.

## When to Use

Load this before choosing or starting a bug-bounty / audit-contest target, and before re-auditing
any surface of a previously examined protocol. It records what has already been verified-negative
so a session is not spent re-deriving the same dismissals.

Consult this BEFORE spending a session on a target. Each entry lists surfaces already
verified-negative with evidence, so they are not re-audited. Re-open an entry only when the
target ships NEW code touching that surface (check commit dates, not listing dates).

Companion skills: `audit-competition-hunt` (acquisition/build/campaign procedure),
`new-feature-bug-hunt` (freshness verification), `bugbounty-target-selection` (rep gates).

## NEAR Intents (HackenProof, 2 programs x $300k) — PARKED, 5 passes, no Critical

Artifacts: `E:/audit/near-intents/NEAR-INTENTS-TRACE.md` (full 5-pass evidence),
`ftv-review.txt` (extracted ToB audit), `survey_launched30.json`.
Repos: `E:/audit/near-intents/intents` (Windows); WSL `Ubuntu-24.04`
`~/audit/near-intents/{omni-bridge,btc-bridge,mpc}`.

Do not re-audit these — each was closed with evidence:

- **defuse engine core** (`contracts/defuse`): signature -> verifying_contract -> deadline ->
  key ownership -> nonce verify+commit chain is complete; `Deltas::finalize()` enforces global
  token conservation (greedy two-pointer matcher, leftover => `UnmatchedDeltas` => whole tx fails).
- **defuse payload/signature layer**: 7-standard dispatch maps curves correctly, per-standard
  digests give domain separation; WebAuthn implements the W3C steps incl. challenge binding.
- **BTC light client**: the deprecated `verify_transaction_inclusion` v1 internal-merkle-node
  weakness is real but the bridge calls **v2** (`satoshi-bridge/src/btc_light_client/mod.rs:240`).
  U256 carry algebra post-fix #683 is correct; ETH2 merkle depth/index come from fork constants,
  not attacker input; Dogecoin AuxPOW shift-wrap is gated by `#[trusted_relayer]`.
- **omni-bridge NEAR**: `fin_transfer_as_dao` is DAO-role-gated; `TokenDeployer` restricts
  bind_token/log_metadata; the `locked_tokens` fix is coherent across bound/deployed/pre-bind states.
- **omni-bridge EVM** (core, Wormhole, Hyperliquid, BridgeToken, SelectivePausable): chain id +
  nonce + accounts bound into the signed payload; slither on Box = 65 contracts / 64 detectors /
  **2 informational** (one a false positive). `SECURITY.md` lists known issues H-01/H-02/L-01..05.
- **omni-bridge Solana**: signature params bind the ACTUAL on-chain mint+recipient keys,
  malleability checked, serialization complete, nonce bitset atomic. The `used_nonces`
  `init_if_needed` front-running edge is **refuted at Anchor-source level** (see lesson below).
- **omni-bridge Aptos/Starknet**: both fin/init/deploy paths sound; Starknet reverses keccak
  endianness and uses 251-bit nonce words correctly.
- **near/mpc**: `threshold-signatures` is a CRATE inside mpc (standalone repo 404s). Five audits.
  ToB-NEARFTV-4 (HIGH, vote spoofing) is **fixed soundly** via `assert_caller_is_signer()`
  (signer == predecessor). A full scan of mutating API methods found **no sibling gap** — the 5
  unguarded ones are permissionless-by-design; `clean_invalid_attestations` protects in-use nodes.

Why parked: mature code (5 MPC audits, SECURITY.md on two legs), every money path consistently
guarded. Odds of a solo Critical are low relative to the effort.

## Aero / dromos-labs metadex — detail pass 1–2 (superseded by PARKED entry below)

Artifacts for the pass-1/2 detail: `E:/audit/aero/AERO-TRACE.md`. Repo
`dromos-labs/metadex-public` @ `2ce1816`, Foundry, solc 0.8.36, ~44.5k LOC in `V3/src`;
`V3/test` is NOT exported. Genuinely fresh code (versioned public releases, relay released most
recently) but six prior audits. The PARKED entry below is the authoritative verdict; everything in
this section is pre-pass-3 evidence kept only for the individual reasoning trails.

Relay surfaces closed with evidence — do not re-derive:

- **Reward accumulator** (`RelayRewardsLib`, `RelayToken`, `RelayBase.onRelayTokenTransfer`):
  hook settles pre-change balances; PT returns early so only YT settles; new holder accrues
  zero and checkpoints at the current index; `notifyReward` reserves with `ceilDiv` so the
  accounted balance covers merged-delta claims; `removeRewardToken` is gated on `index == 0`,
  which closes the checkpoint-underflow/re-add freeze; `claimSettled` is CEI; `pull`/`sweep`
  bounded to the un-accounted balance.
- **Deposit/exit queue** (`QueueLib`): the `toUint128` share cast cannot overflow at realistic
  magnitudes (needs `supply/backing > 2^128/amount`); `registerExit` takes the WHOLE processed
  record and there is NO withdrawal floor (the config NatSpec says so explicitly; the
  `BelowMinimumWithdrawal` error is dead code), so the "holder can always queue its whole free
  position" boundary holds; destinations above `uint72.max` are refused, not truncated.
- **`AllocationLib.extendLock`**: monotonic, touches no backing/supply/index — the accepted
  permissionless lock refresh moves no value.
- **Caller-ordered overdue admission**: real ordering effect, keeper-controlled by design; not
  a conservation break.
- **Whole-V3 slither (Box)**: 295 contracts / 61 detectors / 8 results, ALL
  `msg-value-in-nonpayable` on delegatecall-reached library functions = false positives.

Pass 2 closed these as well:

- **Entrypoints** (`BaseEntrypoint`, `MultiEntrypoint`): KEEPER-gated, router must be
  registry-approved, `tokenIn != tokenOut`, output measured as the entrypoint's own balance
  delta (router untrusted), approval force-reset to 0, leftover read by balance, and idle
  balance bounded by `balanceOf - accountedBalance` so owed rewards/rake are never spent.
  Target/excluded token sets are mutually exclusive and owner-gated.
- **`RelayIcaModule`**: keeper/leaf-config changes are admin + timelock; `_buildApprovals`
  approves exactly the summed per-token leg amounts (the unlimited allowance only wraps the
  sweep leg and is revoked after the batch); the plan is pinned by Hyperlane's
  `keccak(salt || calls)` commitment.
- **`RelayFactory` / `RelayLeafModuleDeployer`**: CREATE2 not clones (immutable bindings would
  otherwise be shared custody); deploy is permissionless and idempotent; factory salt is
  scoped to `msg.sender`, entrypoints must be bound to the predicted address, clone+initialize
  are atomic, and an inert-clone guard reverts if `principalToken()` is zero afterwards.
- **`RelayGovernanceLib`**: slice reads holder principal, Relay VE weight and total supply all
  at the proposal snapshot; per-(governor, proposal, holder) used-weight ledger with CEI;
  fractional params must be exactly 48 bytes and cannot exceed the remaining slice; the cast
  selector is pinned AND payloads under 4 bytes are rejected. `RelayTape` is fail-open
  observability with no fund custody.
- **Pools** (`Pool.sol`, `StablePool`): fees are transferred OUT to `PoolFees`, so balances are
  fee-free and the `_k(balance) >= _k(reserve)` swap check is tight; balances re-read after the
  fee transfer; burn runs the `KIsZero` threshold and mint the `MINIMUM_K` + `MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY`
  floors; `_updateFor` gives a zero-balance user the current index (no retroactive fees).
  `sync()` has no k check but can only RAISE reserves, so the accepted "k==0 drains for free"
  state is unreachable through it.

Unexplored: `gauges`/`voter`/`vpm` (weight routing and fee claims), `metarouter` (command
decoding and the cross-chain leg), `migration` (Aerodrome/Velodrome), `tokenRegistry`,
`splitter`, `hooks`, `art`, and the leaf-side `RelayLeafModule` claim path.

## Aero / dromos-labs metadex (Sherlock bounty 437, $500k Critical) — PARKED, 4 passes

Artifact: `E:/audit/aero/AERO-TRACE.md`; harnesses under `metadex-public/test/`.
Repo `dromos-labs/metadex-public` @ `2ce1816`, Foundry, solc 0.8.36; V3/src = 44.5k LOC;
`V3/test` is NOT published, so harnesses had to be written from scratch. npm on Windows fails with

Do not re-audit these surfaces — each was closed with evidence:

- **Relay core** (queue, rewards, governance, ICA, entrypoints, factory, deployer): reward index
  accounting is solvency-safe (ceil-div accounted balance, pre-change settle, index-gated token
  removal); `_processEntry` share overflow needs an unreachable 3.4e11x backing collapse; there is no
  withdrawal floor by design (an exit takes one deposit whole); `extendLock` moves no accounting;
  the cast selector is pinned with a `<4-byte` guard; clone/deployer races are closed by caller-scoped
  salts, atomic create+initialize, and an inert-clone guard.
- **Pools + voters**: hardened Aerodrome pattern — fees transferred out before the k check, `KIsZero`
  burn guard, `MINIMUM_K` mint guard, `sync` only raises reserves; `withdrawToNFT` conserves weight
  exactly (dust to fee accumulator); `spendableSurplus` is non-decreasing.
- **Metarouter, leaf module, migration, small modules**: transient locker + child-frame allow-revert,
  NFT custody check, bridge-token binding, budget checks, CEI in `Splitter`, hash-bound registry
  review, `LeafVoter` orchestrator/operator gate. All sound.
- **Static**: full-V3 slither = 295 contracts, 61 detectors, 8 results, ALL `msg-value-in-nonpayable`
  on delegatecall library functions from payable entrypoints — false positives.
- **Fuzzing**: two Foundry invariant harnesses (`AeroRewards`, `AeroQueue`) = **409,600 calls**,
  0 violations, with non-vacuous handler counts and sanity tests.

Why parked: six prior audits, every documented invariant held, and the re-survey found no new
fresh-code program (watchlist 534 entries, 0 new launches in 30 days).

## Inverse Finance (Mantis, Ethereum) — CLOSED: JD-01 rejected as intended behaviour

Artifacts: `E:/audit/inverse/findings/inverse-coverage.md` (90-asset scope extraction + full
static verdict map), `JD01-report-en.md`, `Laporan-Temuan-Inverse-Finance-JD01.pdf`.

Scope extracted from the Mantis RSC payload: 89 in-scope, DebtConverter is the only out.

CONFIRMED (Medium, TWO fork PoCs PASS): **JD-01** — `FiRMSlashingModule.slash()`
nets bad debt against `Market.getCollateralValue` (pessimistic 2-day-low `viewPrice`), then
`Market.repay()` reduces debt WITHOUT seizing collateral; slash is permissionless so the
borrower self-calls. PRIMARY PoC: `FiRM/test/slashing/JD01Light.t.sol` (dip only 32.5% on
CF 8500, >15% suffices on CF 9200 markets): borrow 3000, repay to 100, withdrawMax repeatedly
to 0.0616 WETH, dip+recover, pessCV 97.77 < debt 100 < cap 100, juniors pay 2.22 DOLA,
collateral intact. SECONDARY: `FiRM/test/slashing/JD01.t.sol` (98% dip, juniors pay 2905 DOLA).
Fuzzing: 500 runs PASS, observed slashed 541.97 DOLA on 1000 DOLA debt, so `maxCollateralValue` caps `pessCV`, NOT the payout (corrected earlier wrong claim of a 100 DOLA cap). Net-profit PoC `FiRM/test/slashing/JD01NetProfit.t.sol` PASS: DOLA/WETH/escrow balances unchanged, debt drops by exactly the junior payout, net worth gain equals payout.

**FINAL VERDICT (2026-11-23): REJECTED by the platform.** Team reply: slash() intentionally covers only debt above collateral value; absorbing bad debt after a price drop is jrDOLA's role and junior depositors earn revenue for it; pessimistic-oracle low valuation is intended; the scenario needs a market move the borrower cannot cause; the pattern was reviewed before. Submission `cmwqr8chg000a08jrhjxgm52w` status `rejected`. Three follow-ups were sent (net-profit, escalation with developer comments, and a hunter acknowledgement); all failed to change the call. Do NOT re-report JD-01 or re-argue this mechanism on this program: the owner has explicitly classified it as intended. The developer comments in `FiRMSlashingModule.sol` ('avoid unliquidateable debt used to drain jDOLA depositors', 'want positions liquidated before repaying bad debt') were presented and still rejected, so an intended-behaviour rebuttal from source comments has no traction here. Historical fork PoC without mock could not be produced: on 21 Aug 2026 (block 25798000) `viewPrice` was dampened only 3.8%, far below the >15% needed at CF 8500; other scanned blocks showed ratio 10000.

Factory contracts are NOT in Mantis scope. NO NEW FINDING from this re-pass. Treat Inverse Finance as fully exhausted unless a new audited-relevant contract ships.

## Exactly Protocol (Cantina, Optimism + Base) — PARKED 2026-11-23, no payable finding

Program: `exactly-bug-bounty`, top reward $25k Critical (10% economic damage, needs about $250k loss), High $5-10k. 54 contracts, self-triaged, $50 deposit refundable for legitimate reports, KYC required, PoC mandatory for High/Critical. Busy competition (60-67 submissions in 11 days). Full evidence: `E:/audit/exactly/verdict-exactly-2026-11-23.md`, fork PoC `E:/audit/exactly/poc/` (6 tests pass at Base block 61058483), scope guard `E:/audit/scope-programs/exactly-cantina.md` (54 active rules).

**The shortlist claim that Oct 2026 commits were fresh functional code was wrong.** `8ac093a1` (15 Oct setup wARS), `13d99979` (19 Oct upgrade auditor/debt roller, deploy flash loaner), `80c28e11` (22 Oct tokenized stock setup) and `86b3a641` (28 Oct deploy stock markets) changed only deployment JSON, hardhat config, `.openzeppelin` state and changesets. No `.sol` source. `Market.sol` last changed 21 Apr 2026, `Auditor.sol` 15 Sep 2026 (NatSpec only), `InterestRateModel.sol` 22 Oct 2025. The features behind the deployments were audited by ABDK: Non-Collateral Markets (17 Sep 2026, PR #815 `6c022f3`, 0 Critical/Major/Moderate) and Flash Loan Adapter + Inverse Price Feed (19 Oct 2026, `371e41a` fixed in `9bf6024`, 16 Minor only). Both PDFs are linked from the program page as known issues, so CVF-1..6, adjustFactor 0, inverse-price staleness and FlashLoanAdapter leftover sweep are all known and non-payable.

**Lead `ProposalManager.checkLiquidity` was tested and retracted.** It ignores `nonCollateral` (source unchanged since 1 Oct 2025, selector `0xcd36d9fc` present in Base `0xB92E0A6E...` bytecode) and passes for a wARS-only or empty account on Base fork block 61058483. But `Auditor.accountLiquidity` gives wARS zero borrowing power, a real floating borrow at Base USDC reverts `0x15d58176` (`InsufficientAccountLiquidity`), `ExaPlugin.collectCredit` forwards `msg.sender` as borrower so there is no caller bypass, and `preExecutionChecker` never calls `checkLiquidity`. Impact stops at a failed card transaction or over-broad server authorisation; griefing and best practice are excluded. The observation is also published in ABDK p.26. No value can be stolen, frozen or borrowed unbacked. Do NOT re-report.

Other rejected angles: PriceFeedInverse/PriceFeedwARS staleness and inverse error (ABDK CVF-3/CVF-5), FlashLoanAdapter no return check (CVF-1, client says both callers repay exact amount), DebtRoller vs Auditor markets() tuple order (admin/governance), `adjustFactor=0` freeze (admin-only), `deploy/mocks/Assets.ts` missing live-network guard (config/test file). Remaining untested corner: inverse USD/ARS feed under extreme peso move, but that is ABDK CVF-3/CVF-5 so expected payout is low. Reopen only on a new implementation or scope change after 23 Nov 2026.

## Cross-checking a shared target list against prior work

When handed a pasted list of bounty programs and asked which ones are untouched,
classify every entry from evidence, not from memory:

1. Parse each entry into (program name, platform, announcement URL or status id).
   Match by that identity, not by project name: a build/integration bounty and a
   bug bounty for the same protocol are different programs, and a closed build
   bounty does not mark the bug bounty as worked. One org can host several live
   bounties with different slugs and scope, so a rejection or parked verdict on
   one slug says nothing about a sibling slug: compare the exact slug and the
   in-scope assets before transferring a verdict.
2. Batch the history check. For more than a few targets, query the Hermes
   `state.db` read-only with sqlite3 (`sqlite3.connect('file:' + path +
   '?mode=ro', uri=True)`) and group `messages` by anchor, session and role
   instead of issuing one `session_search` call per name.
3. Anchor on distinctive strings: platform + program name, an announcement
   status id, or a repo path. Never substring-scan short generic tokens like
   `exactly`, `cosmos`, `metric` or `raac` — case-insensitive matches hit
   ordinary prose and unrelated strings, so every hit needs context checked.
4. Promote a hit to "worked on" only with artifact evidence: a clone under
   `E:/audit` or `E:/bug bounty`, a TRACE/notes/verdict file, a fuzz harness, a
   PoC, or an entry in this register. A mention in a research PDF, aggregator
   dump or scouting list is a mention, not work.
5. Report both buckets with counts and evidence paths, and label depth
   separately: surveyed with no finding, active campaign, or finding submitted.
   State plainly when a program appears only in a list.
6. Close with a short numbered set of next actions (vet one target, rank the
   untouched ones by PoC feasibility, or resume the active campaign); this user
   picks from numbered options.

Absence from this register is not proof a target is untouched: confirm with
session history and repo directories before telling the user it has never been
worked on.

## Procedure lives in the companion skills

Do not re-derive campaign procedure from this register. It is in `audit-competition-hunt`:
acquisition and build (Windows npm git-dep workaround, public exports missing the test tree),
reading `SECURITY.md`/`Known_issues`/`audits/` first and mining accepted-behaviour entries for the
invariants they assert, working an audit finding as a lead plus the sibling-gap guard scan,
non-vacuous invariant campaigns, Anchor `init_if_needed` semantics, and Box offload quirks.
Code-age vs listing-age verification is in `new-feature-bug-hunt`; rep/KYC/deposit gates in
`bugbounty-target-selection`.

Register-specific rules:
- Before recording "no source available" for a target, search the protocol's public audits repository and read its newest PDF. Audit reports supply function names, patch references, known-issue status and live-state coordinates even when the source repo is private; skipping that step parks a target on a false premise. Confirm the newest audited patches are present in the deployed ELF by grepping distinctive error strings, and treat acknowledged findings as coordinates for a NEW variant, never as findings themselves. When a PDF has no text layer, render its pages with `pymupdf` from the project venv and read the rendered images with vision analysis before closing the known-issues list; an unreadable audit is not the same as an absent audit.
- Record a verdict with its EVIDENCE PATH and the call/evaluation count, so a future session can
  trust the negative without re-running it.
- When the fresh-target survey yields no payable target, say so plainly and offer monitoring
  instead of forcing a weak one. A demo/preview contest, a post-audit Critical-only contest, or a
  points-based reward is not a substitute for a freshly deployed, unaudited, payable scope —
  spending a session on one is worse than reporting that the window is empty.
- An empty 30-day launch survey is not automatically an empty window: also check live payable
  programs outside the aggregator and watchlist that already have local source and an unfinished
  phase. A self-hosted program qualifies when its official docs state both a reward and a smart
  contract scope; verify those from the docs, not from an aggregator. Prefer that over forcing a
  weak fresh listing, because the code and the reconnaissance work are already on disk.
- Before starting a target whose source is not already local, check verified-source availability
  for its in-scope addresses and record `exact_match` status plus the bytecode-match result.
  A tree that does not byte-match deployment makes the target unauditable until verified source
  is obtained; do not spend a session deriving findings from it. If Sourcify returns 400 and the
  address is not a proxy, check Blockscout's smart-contract API before calling the contract
  unidentified — a scope can mix Sourcify-verified and Blockscout-only entries.
- When new code re-opens a parked target, extend that protocol's existing entry with the new
  surface's verdict; do not create a second entry for the same protocol. Search the register for
  the protocol name before inserting anything: long register files make an existing entry easy to
  miss, and a duplicate section leaves contradictory verdicts for the same protocol.
- A target whose listing is new but whose pinned code is old is not a fresh surface — note the
  code age in the entry so the next selection pass does not shortlist it again.

### bounty-hunt-pipeline

*Sumber: `installed` - `skills/02-recon-targeting/bounty-hunt-pipeline/SKILL.md`*

> Use to route a bounty engagement P0-P6 end to end.

# Bounty hunt pipeline (P0 to P6)

One router for a full engagement. It does not duplicate any phase skill: it names the phase, the skill that owns it, the artifact that must exist before the next phase, and the condition that sends you back.

## When to Use

- Starting a new target, or resuming one after a gap, and the next step is unclear.
- Deciding whether a candidate is worth a phase transition.
- Not for a single-finding question (that is `finding-validation-gate`) and not for readiness of the arsenal (`skill-library-audit`).

## Phases

| Phase | Owner skill | Artifact to produce | Gate forward |
|---|---|---|---|
| P0 Target | `bugbounty-target-selection`, `bounty-target-verdicts` | Gate sheet: rep, KYC, PoC rule, payout band, prior verdicts, freshness | All five recorded, and not already parked at HEAD |
| P1 Scope | `chain-scope-guard` (contracts) or the live brief transcript (web2) | `scope.json` with every in-scope id and rule | `--audit` passes; a three-line quote of the accepted-impact clause |
| P2 Recon | `new-feature-bug-hunt`, `web-api-bounty-hunt` | Asset and entry-point inventory, code age, deployment map, local-vs-deployed delta when a deployment exists | One inventory row per scope entry; every instruction or route present in only one of repo/deployment recorded |
| P3 Hunt | `evm-bounty-source-audit` or `web-api-bounty-hunt`, spokes only as routed | Test matrix plus coverage ledger (`redteam-mindset`) | All sweep classes recorded |
| P4 Validate | `finding-validation-gate` | Gate sheet per candidate, microscope on the strongest | Every survivor has a PoC or a named park condition |
| P5 Evidence | `evidence-hygiene` | Redacted screenshots, sanitized HAR or tx bundle, SHA256 manifest | Manifest verifies, secret scan clean |
| P6 Deliver | `report-writing`, plus `bugcrowd-reporting` on Bugcrowd | Paste-ready draft plus an audited send kit shown to the operator | Every kit item matches current status; operator approves; submission ID recorded |

## Routing fork

- Contracts (static source, fork, fuzz): P3 is `evm-bounty-source-audit`. Add `defi-bounty-predive` for go/no-go and `meme-coin-audit` only on token scopes. Never both checklists at once.
- Web or API (live HTTP): P3 is `web-api-bounty-hunt`, with `web-api-authz-matrix` for object and role boundaries, `race-condition-web-api` for one-use flows, and `cspt-client-side-path-hunt` when a URL value reaches a client-built request path.
- Mobile or binary: `android-app-security-review` or `rea-static-analysis` at P3, with the same P1 and P5 rules.
- Substrate/Rust node source with pallet-based scope (for example a self-hosted node bounty): P3 is read-only static review of the pallet named in the newest release-prep commit, entered through a tag-to-tag diff so only the fresh lines are hunted. P1 is the program's own brief transcript, not a chain-address guard, when the program takes reports by email. Do not install the wasm32/Substrate build stack before an in-scope candidate exists; when the operator authorizes a runtime build, offload it to Colab or Kaggle rather than compiling locally. WHY: the runtime build is the expensive step and the fresh pallet diff is where the least-reviewed code sits.

## Send-backs

- P4 kills the only candidate: return to P3, next sweep class, not to P0.
- P1 loses an asset the finding depends on: the finding becomes a chain at P4, or dies.
- A new commit lands on an in-scope surface after P5: restart P2 for that surface only, then P4.

## Non-negotiables

- Every phase writes a file under `E:/audit/<target>/`. Chat is not storage.
- On any "how many bugs / what is new / what is left" question, reconcile first:
  search prior sessions for the target, inventory every findings directory
  including any final audit report and coverage ledger, and rank the newest
  verified artifact above older drafts. Report confirmed, retracted and
  submittable counts separately. WHY: a parallel session can retract a finding
  or add one after the current context was written, and an outdated count sends
  the operator to submit a dead finding.
- At P6, audit the send kit itself. Every panduan, paste file, bundle README
  and checksum manifest must agree with current finding status; remove
  retracted and disqualified items and regenerate the manifest. WHY: the
  operator copies the kit, not the chat conclusion, so a stale bundle is an
  active submission hazard.
- No phase starts with its artifact from the previous phase still empty. A skipped artifact is the usual cause of a wrong report.
- When a phase is blocked on an operator-side dependency (account, session, deposit, KYC), still write that phase's artifact with an explicit blocked status and the named unblocking condition, then write each downstream artifact as an empty placeholder with `[TOFILL]` and no invented finding. WHY: a missing artifact invites the next session to jump the gate and manufacture a report to fill the hole.
- Do not append a verdict to `bounty-target-verdicts` for a target that is still active with no finding. Reserve that register for submitted findings and closed negative verdicts with evidence paths. WHY: a parked label on a live target stops a future session from resuming it.
- Account steps (signup, KYC, deposit, public submit) belong to the operator; hand them a numbered list, never a paragraph.
- A program rule requiring the operator to personally validate the finding and run the PoC is a P6 gate, not a P3 blocker: continue the read-only hunt, build PoCs and drafts, and mark P6 blocked with the operator's own validation as the named unblock. Never submit from the agent side.
- A parked verdict in `bounty-target-verdicts` reopens only on new code touching the parked surface, checked by commit date.
- Do not skip P0 to save time on a listing badge: listing age is not code age.
- Never park an in-scope program as unauditable for lack of source before searching the local audit corpus and the SDK IDL. A private repository still leaves public audit PDFs, and those name the functions, file paths, patch identifiers and acknowledged-versus-resolved status; that is enough to rank a live hunt without the source tree. WHY: "no public repo" is a statement about git access, not about the amount of specification available, and a parked lane with an unread audit is a coverage hole that survives into later sessions.
- When the operator asks what changed or what was under-dug, run a freshness pass before answering: remote HEADs of every cloned repo, the protocol's own config API listing, the program page's last-updated field, and the local audit directory. Report the deltas with evidence, then act on the highest-value gap in the same turn rather than delivering an inventory alone.
- When the target is a live deployment with a public repo, diff the deployed instruction/route set against the repo's list before P3. A handler present only in the deployment is unaudited by every published review; a handler present only in the repo does not exist on chain and a PoC built on it reverts. Also re-read offsets out of the deployment (an SDK IDL, the program's own error text), never out of a repo struct — a drifting layout gives reads that look plausible and are wrong.

## Close-out

Coverage ledger, verdict per lane, carry-overs, monitor jobs if freshness matters, and the verdict appended to `bounty-target-verdicts`. Then stop; no padding.

If the engagement is blocked before a verdict exists, close with the carry-over list and the named unblocking step instead. A status file that names each phase, its owner skill, its artifact, and its gate is the router's own output; keep it beside the phase artifacts so a resumed session starts from the gate, not from chat history.
